artiest/mike-love.text:
Mike Love is the singer and lyricist of The Beach Boys, born in 1941 in Los Angeles. He founded the group with his cousins Brian, Dennis and Carl Wilson and their friend Al Jardine. Love sang in a nasal baritone on most recordings and was usually the frontman on stage.

Together with Brian Wilson he wrote fifteen songs that reached the American top 40, among them Fun, Fun, Fun, I Get Around, California Girls and Good Vibrations. His lyrics were mostly about surfing, cars and falling in love, and so shaped the sunny image of California for which the band became known. Kokomo (1988), which Love co-wrote, became the group's only number 1 hit without any input from Brian Wilson. That same year The Beach Boys were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

In 1968 Love travelled to Rishikesh in India to learn Transcendental Meditation from Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, at the same time as the Beatles. In 1971 he became a teacher of the technique himself. According to Love, he helped Paul McCartney there with the lyrics of Back in the U.S.S.R. In the 1990s he brought a lawsuit against Brian Wilson and was eventually recognised as co-writer of 35 songs. After the death of Carl Wilson in 1998 he was the only one granted the right to tour as The Beach Boys.
artiest/mike-love.listen: Listen in Good Vibrations to the low, nasal voice of Mike Love in the verses. Notice how it gives way to the chorus with its high voices and the humming, swooping sound of the electro-theremin.

artiest/mike-oldfield.text:
Mike Oldfield was born in Reading in 1953 and is an English musician, songwriter and producer, best known for his debut album Tubular Bells from 1973. He began playing guitar at the age of ten, learned by copying songs by folk guitarists such as Bert Jansch and John Renbourn, and was a slow reader of sheet music. From 1967 to 1970 he formed the folk duo Sallyangie with his sister Sally, who recorded the album Children of the Sun. He then played bass with Kevin Ayers, before beginning work on Tubular Bells in 1971.

His demo tape with a long instrumental piece, at first called Opus One, eventually caught the attention of Richard Branson, who made it the first release of his new label Virgin. Tubular Bells was released on 25 May 1973. Oldfield played more than twenty instruments on a layered recording that passed through many styles. When the opening was used in the film The Exorcist, the theme became a top hit in the United States. Hergest Ridge in 1974, Ommadawn in 1975 and Incantations in 1978 followed. In the late 1970s he began touring and made more song-oriented records, such as Platinum, QE2 and Five Miles Out. His most successful album of that period was Crises from 1983, with the worldwide hit Moonlight Shadow, sung by Maggie Reilly. Tubular Bells II in 1992 and Tubular Bells III in 1998 came later.

Oldfield is first and foremost a guitarist, but also plays keyboards and percussion and sings. He showed that a studio album, with the overdubs of a single man, could achieve the sound of a full orchestra, and for a time he made instrumental music a bestseller.
artiest/mike-oldfield.listen: Listen to the beginning of Tubular Bells and notice how the piano riff repeats while another instrument is added each time: which sounds can you count?

artiest/mike-osborne.text:
Mike Osborne was born in 1941 in Hereford and was an English jazz alto saxophonist, pianist and clarinettist. He attended Wycliffe College in Gloucestershire and studied at the Guildhall School of Music. From 1962 to 1972 he played in the band of Mike Westbrook. During those years he also worked with musicians such as Michael Gibbs, Mike Cooper, Stan Tracey, Kenny Wheeler, Humphrey Lyttelton, Alan Skidmore and John Surman. In the 1960s and 1970s he was a member of Brotherhood of Breath, the big band built around the South African pianist Chris McGregor.

His quintet recorded the album Outback, with McGregor on piano, Harry Miller on bass and Louis Moholo on drums. He also made Border Crossing and All Night Long (Live at Willisau) with his trio for the label Ogun, and recorded the record Original with Stan Tracey, released in 1973, and the duo Tandem at the Bracknell Festival. Later albums included Marcel's Muse and Shapes in 1995. Force of Nature was released in 2008, and Dawn in 2015.

Health problems ended his career in 1982. He returned to Hereford and lived there in a care home, where he died in 2007. Osborne belonged to the generation of British jazz musicians who combined free jazz and big-band work, and showed that the saxophone in England could acquire a rough and lyrical voice of its own.
artiest/mike-osborne.listen: Listen to the album Outback and notice the interplay of the alto sax with the rhythm section: how high and sharp does Osborne sound, and when does he give the others room?

artiest/mike-pinder.text:
Mike Pinder was a keyboard player and co-founder of The Moody Blues. He was born in 1941 in Erdington, a district of Birmingham. Before becoming a musician he worked for about eighteen months as a development technician at Streetly Electronics, the factory in Birmingham that built the first British Mellotrons. In May 1964 he left to start The Moody Blues with Ray Thomas, Denny Laine, Clint Warwick and Graeme Edge. Their version of Go Now reached number 1 in England in 1965.

Pinder is best known for his work with the Mellotron, a keyboard instrument that plays a short piece of recorded tape for each key, of strings or a choir, for example. Because he knew the machine technically, he was able to give it a permanent place in the rock of the 1960s. On albums such as Days of Future Passed (1967) and In Search of the Lost Chord (1968) the Mellotron became the heart of the group's sound. Pinder was the band's chief arranger until 1978 and also wrote and sang songs himself, such as The Sunset and Om. His Melancholy Man became a number 1 hit in France.

In 1978 he left the group, after the album Octave. He made solo albums, such as The Promise (1976), and in the 1980s and 1990s worked as an adviser for the computer company Atari. In 2018 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with The Moody Blues. Pinder died in California in 2024, aged 82.
artiest/mike-pinder.listen: Listen in Nights in White Satin to the floating string sound behind the vocals: that is Mike Pinder's Mellotron. Notice how that sound swells in the chorus and makes the song bigger than an ordinary rock band.

artiest/mike-post.text: Mike Post was born in Berkeley in 1944. He began as an arranger and producer in pop music and at the age of 23 won a Grammy for his arrangement of Classical Gas by Mason Williams. He then concentrated on television. Together with the composer Pete Carpenter he wrote the music for many American series. The theme tunes of The Rockford Files (1974) and Hill Street Blues (1981) both reached number ten on the American chart. Magnum, P.I., The A-Team, L.A. Law and NYPD Blue followed, among others. For Law & Order (1990) he also devised the short 'dun dun' sound between scenes.
artiest/mike-post.listen: Notice how short and direct a TV theme is: in a few seconds a catchy motif, a pop rhythm and a recognisable instrument set the tone for the whole series.

artiest/mike-shinoda.text:
Mike Shinoda is a rapper, singer, songwriter, producer and graphic designer. He was born in 1977 in Panorama City, a district of Los Angeles, and grew up in Agoura Hills in California. At high school he was in the same class as Brad Delson and Rob Bourdon, with whom he started Linkin Park in 1996; the first version of the band was called Xero. He then studied graphic design and illustration.

In Linkin Park, Shinoda was the counterpart of the singer Chester Bennington. Where Bennington sang and screamed, Shinoda rapped. He also played rhythm guitar and keyboards, wrote most of the songs and co-produced. That combination of rap, heavy guitars and electronics is characteristic of the nu metal of around 2000. The debut Hybrid Theory (2000) was a huge success. In 2004 Shinoda produced Collision Course, a collaboration between Linkin Park and Jay-Z, which won a Grammy in 2006.

To show his hip-hop background, in 2004 he started the side project Fort Minor. From the album The Rising Tied (2005), Where'd You Go reached number four on the American Hot 100. After Bennington's death in July 2017, Shinoda made the solo album Post Traumatic (2018), on which he works through his grief. He is also a painter and has exhibited at the Japanese American National Museum in Los Angeles. In 2022 he won a Grammy for his remix of Passenger by Deftones.
artiest/mike-shinoda.listen: Listen in In the End to the division of roles: Shinoda raps the verses over a simple, repeated piano figure, while Bennington sings and screams the chorus. Notice how the guitars only come in fully at the chorus.

artiest/mike-stock.text:
Mike Stock is an English songwriter, producer and musician. He was born in 1951 in Margate and grew up in Swanley, in Kent. He taught himself to play piano and guitar and was writing songs at the age of seven. The Beatles, but also writers such as Irving Berlin and Rodgers and Hammerstein, gave him a great love of the pop song. For years he played with bands in clubs and hotels every night. In the early 1980s he brought the guitarist Matt Aitken into his band. In 1984 the two began working only in the studio, and shortly afterwards they formed the trio Stock Aitken Waterman with Pete Waterman.

The trio began with Hi-NRG for the dance clubs and in 1985 scored a first number 1 hit with You Spin Me Round (Like a Record) by Dead or Alive. In their new studio in the Borough, the Hit Factory, Venus by Bananarama, Respectable by Mel and Kim and Never Gonna Give You Up by Rick Astley (1987) followed. For Kylie Minogue, Stock and Aitken wrote I Should Be So Lucky (1988) in forty minutes. Stock was above all the man of melodies and chords. The SAW sound consisted of a tight drum machine, glossy synthesizers and a chorus you know after hearing it once. In 1989 the trio had seven number 1 hits in Great Britain.

After Aitken's departure in 1991, Stock worked with Waterman for another two years. He then started his own label, Love This Records, and had success with Nicki French and with Robson & Jerome. He is regarded as one of the most successful songwriters in Great Britain.
artiest/mike-stock.listen: Listen to I Should Be So Lucky by Kylie Minogue. Notice how simple the melody is and how often the chorus comes back, above a tight drum machine and synthesizers.

artiest/mike-stoller.text:
Mike Stoller is an American composer and producer. He was born in 1933 in Queens, New York, and with the lyricist Jerry Leiber formed one of the most important songwriting duos in the history of popular music. Stoller wrote the music, Leiber the words. They met in 1950 in Los Angeles, where Stoller played piano after school and Leiber worked in a record shop. They shared a love of blues and rhythm and blues.

In 1952 they wrote Hound Dog for the blues singer Big Mama Thornton, who had a hit with it a year later. Elvis Presley's version from 1956 became much bigger still. Stoller only heard the news when he had been rescued in New York from a sunken ship, and asked in astonishment: Elvis who? They went on to write for Presley, among others, Jailhouse Rock, Loving You and King Creole. At Atlantic Records they were also allowed to work for other labels, which in effect made them the first independent producers. For The Coasters they made funny, theatrical songs about teenage life, such as Searchin', Yakety Yak and Charlie Brown. For The Drifters they produced songs such as On Broadway, and with Ben E. King they wrote Stand By Me.

In the 1960s they founded Red Bird Records, where girl groups such as the Shangri-Las and the Dixie Cups scored hits. A young Phil Spector learned the trade in their studio. Leiber and Stoller wrote or co-wrote more than seventy hits. In 1987 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/mike-stoller.listen: Listen to Hound Dog by Big Mama Thornton from 1953. Notice how she delivers the song as raw blues, and then compare that with the faster rock 'n' roll version by Elvis Presley.

artiest/miki-matsubara.text:
Miki Matsubara was born in 1959 in Kishiwada, Osaka, the daughter of a jazz singer. She learned to play piano at the age of three and became interested in rock as a teenager. In 1977, at seventeen, she went alone to Tokyo to become a singer. There she was discovered by the pianist Yuzuru Sera, who saw her playing in clubs such as Birdland in Roppongi.

In 1979 her debut single Mayonaka no Door (Stay With Me) was released. It was an immediate hit and reached number twenty-eight on the Oricon chart. Other well-known songs were Neat na gogo san-ji, which was heard in a Shiseido advertisement, and The Winner. For the albums ―CUPID― (1981) and Myself (1982) she worked in Los Angeles with the fusion group Dr. Strut, who accompanied her. Later she also made a jazz album, Blue Eyes, with, among others, Love for Sale and You've Got a Friend. Matsubara had a mezzo-soprano voice.

In 2000 she stopped making music after being diagnosed with cancer, and she died in 2004 at the age of 44. Since 2020, Mayonaka no Door has become popular worldwide via TikTok and the revival of city pop. City pop is smooth Japanese pop music with jazz, funk and soul. In this way the singer, who during her lifetime was known mainly in Japan, found a new audience.
artiest/miki-matsubara.listen: Listen to Mayonaka no Door (Stay With Me) and notice the way her voice floats through the jazzy chords and the funky bass line. What makes the singing both cool and fiery?

artiest/mikis-theodorakis.text: Mikis Theodorakis (1925–2021) was born on the Greek island of Chios. He studied at the Athens Conservatoire and then in Paris, where he took music analysis with Olivier Messiaen. He wrote more than a thousand works and often mixed the symphony orchestra with Greek folk instruments and popular melodies in them. His music for Zorba the Greek (1964) became famous. To his theme, Anthony Quinn and Alan Bates dance the sirtaki on the beach. During the military dictatorship (1967–1974) his music was banned in Greece. He was arrested and in 1970 went into exile in Paris. For Costa-Gavras he wrote Z (1969), for which he received a BAFTA, and État de siège (1972). In America he made the music for Serpico (1973).
artiest/mikis-theodorakis.listen: Notice the bouzouki and the tempo: in the dance from Zorba the melody begins slowly and the tempo keeps rising.

artiest/miklos-rozsa.text: Miklós Rózsa was born in Budapest in 1907 and studied in Leipzig. Throughout his life he continued to write concert music as well and brought Hungarian folk music into his style. Via London, where he worked for the producer Alexander Korda, he came to Hollywood with The Thief of Bagdad (1940). In the 1940s he defined the sound of film noir, with harsh, sharp chords in Double Indemnity (1944) and The Killers (1946). For Spellbound (1945) he used the theremin, an electronic instrument, for the confused mind of the protagonist, and won an Oscar. Later he wrote music for monumental historical films, such as Ben-Hur (1959), which brought him his third Oscar.
artiest/miklos-rozsa.listen: Notice the sharp, dissonant chords and the eerie glissandi of the theremin, and compare them with the solemn marches from Ben-Hur.

artiest/milan-hlavsa.text:
Milan Hlavsa, nicknamed Mejla, was a Czech bassist and songwriter from Prague. He was born in 1951 and was an apprentice butcher when he founded The Plastic People of the Universe in 1968, shortly after the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia. He was seventeen at the time. A year earlier a friend had introduced him to the music of The Velvet Underground and Frank Zappa, and those two became his great models. As founder he was also the group's principal composer.

In communist Czechoslovakia, Western music was severely restricted. In 1970 the authorities withdrew the band's professional licence. The members took jobs in forestry and carried on playing, outside the official circuit. They belonged to what was called druhá kultura, the second culture: art that existed without the permission of the state. After a festival of that movement, members were arrested and tried; three went to prison and the former member Paul Wilson was expelled from the country. Hlavsa himself escaped punishment. For Václav Havel and others, the trial was a reason to found Charter 77, the movement that called the government to account over human rights.

In 1988 the band was allowed to perform openly again, but it fell apart shortly afterwards. Hlavsa started Půlnoc, who released the album City of Hysteria in America in 1991. At Havel's suggestion he brought the Plastic People back together in 1997, for the twentieth anniversary of Charter 77. In 1999 they played at the White House, together with Lou Reed. Hlavsa died in January 2001 of lung cancer, aged 49.
artiest/milan-hlavsa.listen: Listen to the album Egon Bondy's Happy Hearts Club Banned by The Plastic People of the Universe. Notice Hlavsa's simple, repeated bass lines and the raw, unpolished sound, which shows how closely the band had listened to The Velvet Underground.

artiest/miles-davis.text: Miles Davis grew up in East St. Louis and came to New York in 1944 to study at the Juilliard School. Dizzy Gillespie was his example, but Miles chose a quieter, more restrained tone. He played in Charlie Parker's quintet. He changed jazz several times: with Birth of the Cool (1949), with his quintet with John Coltrane (1955), with Kind of Blue (1959), with his second quintet (1964) and with the electric music of Bitches Brew (1970). He often used a mute, which made his sound vulnerable. He repeatedly chose young musicians who later became bandleaders themselves, such as Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter and John McLaughlin.
artiest/miles-davis.listen: Notice the space between the notes: Miles plays little, and every note counts.

artiest/mili-balakirev.text:
Mili Balakirev, in the usual spelling Mily Balakirev, was born in 1837 in Nizhny Novgorod and was a Russian composer, pianist and conductor. He is best known because he stimulated musical nationalism and encouraged more famous colleagues. As a boy he had piano lessons from his mother, and later from Karl Eisrach, who introduced him to the music of Chopin and Glinka. The music lover Alexander Ulybyshev took him under his wing. Balakirev studied mathematics in Kazan and in 1855 met Glinka in St Petersburg, who rated his talent highly, although he found his technique lacking.

After Glinka's death in 1857, Balakirev felt that Russia should have a musical school of its own, free of Southern and Western European influence. In the late 1850s and early 1860s, together with the critic Vladimir Stasov, he brought together the composers known as The Five or The Mighty Handful: Alexander Borodin, César Cui, Modest Mussorgsky and Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. For a time he was the only professional musician in the group. He was opposed to academic training and held that you had to learn by composing straight away.

He often completed his own major works years after starting them. He began his First Symphony in 1864 and only finished it in 1897; he began his Second Symphony in 1900 and it was completed in 1908. An exception is the Oriental piano piece Islamey, which he wrote quickly and which is still popular with virtuosos. Balakirev died in 1910. Many ideas that are associated with Rimsky-Korsakov or Borodin came from him.
artiest/mili-balakirev.listen: Listen to Islamey for piano and notice the rapid repetitions and the big leaps: how do the wild passages alternate with the slow, songlike middle section?

artiest/milli-vanilli.text:
Milli Vanilli was a pop duo that formed in Munich in 1988, consisting of Fab Morvan and Rob Pilatus. Their music combined pop, rap, rhythm and blues, disco and dance. Pilatus came from Munich, Morvan from Paris. They met in a discotheque in Los Angeles and found each other again in Munich, where they bonded over their experience as Black young men in European cities. The German producer Frank Farian recorded a cover of Girl You Know It's True, a song by Numarx, with session singers such as Charles Shaw and John Davis. When it became a hit in Europe, he asked Morvan and Pilatus to pose as the singers.

In 1988 All or Nothing was released in Europe. Arista Records released it in the United States in 1989 as Girl You Know It's True, with Blame It on the Rain as an extra track. The album spent eight weeks at number one on the Billboard 200 and produced three number one singles. In 1990 they won three American Music Awards and a Grammy.

Then came the exposure. Because of their French and German accents and a malfunction during a performance, rumours spread that they did not sing themselves. In November 1990 Farian confirmed that other singers had done the vocals. The records were pulled from the radio and the Grammy was revoked. Farian released The Moment of Truth in 1991 as The Real Milli Vanilli. Rob & Fab followed in 1993. Pilatus later died of an overdose. The case changed the discussion about lip-syncing and about what is real in pop music.
artiest/milli-vanilli.listen: Listen to Girl You Know It's True and notice the voice and the rhythm: can you hear the smooth studio production, and what does that say about who is actually singing on the record?

artiest/millie-small.text:
Millie Small was born in 1947 in Clarendon, Jamaica, the daughter of an overseer on a sugar plantation, and was one of thirteen children. She began her career at the age of twelve by winning the talent contest Vere Johns Opportunity Hour, like many Jamaican singers of that time. She then recorded with Roy Panton, as the duo Roy & Millie, with producers such as Roy Robinson, Coxsone Dodd and Lindon Pottinger. They had local hits, including We'll Meet, and in 1963 Marie.

In London she first recorded Don't You Know, which made little impression. For her next recording Chris Blackwell brought in the guitarist and arranger Ernest Ranglin. He arranged My Boy Lollipop in the newly popular ska. In 1964 the song reached number two in both the British and American charts and sold more than seven million copies. It was the first big hit for Island Records, although it was released on the Fontana label, and it made Small an international star at seventeen. The album More Millie was released in 1964 with arrangements by Ranglin, in the United States under the title My Boy Lollipop. She appeared on the Beatles television programme Around the Beatles and made a world tour in 1965.

Her follow-up single Sweet William was less successful, and Bloodshot Eyes was her last British hit in 1965. Time Will Tell was released in 1970. She moved to Singapore in 1971 and returned to Great Britain in 1973. Millie Small died in 2020. She brought ska to a worldwide audience and paved the way for Jamaican music in British pop history.
artiest/millie-small.listen: Listen to My Boy Lollipop and notice the offbeat of the guitar and the high, playful voice: can you hear how ska makes the song skip along?

artiest/milt-franklyn.text:
Milt Franklyn was born in New York in 1897 as Milton Julius Frumkin. When he was three the family moved to Salt Lake City, where he went to high school and studied for a year at the University of Utah. He was junior tennis champion of Utah for six years. He then studied for two years in Berkeley, and began at the University of Pennsylvania when he was called up for the First World War. Because he played several instruments, he joined a band in San Francisco and played in hotels for a few years. He then led an orchestra of his own of nine men, which played under various names.

In 1936 he joined Warner Bros. Cartoons as arranger for Carl Stalling, and in 1954 he became musical director. He wrote his scores at home, early in the morning. The first cartoon in which he was credited as composer was Bugs and Thugs from 1954, although he himself estimated that by then he was already working on his 599th cartoon for Warner. His music belongs to the Looney Tunes featuring, among others, Bugs Bunny and Tweety. In 1954 he joined ASCAP.

He died in 1962 of a heart attack while working on the music for a Tweety cartoon, The Jet Cage. He wrote the first two minutes himself, the rest was written by William Lava, his successor as musical director. His music was later also heard in Bugs Bunny on Broadway. Franklyn showed how in a cartoon the music can follow every movement on the screen: a piece of a few minutes in which sound, gag and tempo coincide.
artiest/milt-franklyn.listen: Listen to the music of a Looney Tunes cartoon by Franklyn and notice how every sound on the screen is followed by an instrument: what do you hear for a fall, a jump or a chase?

artiest/milt-jackson.text: The vibraphonist Milt Jackson, from Detroit, was brought to New York by Dizzy Gillespie in 1945 and played in his band and sextet. He made the vibraphone a bebop instrument. By slowing down the rotating discs in the resonator tubes, he gave his vibraphone a warm, singing vibrato. His nickname was 'Bags'. From 1952 to 1974, and again from 1981, he played in the Modern Jazz Quartet. There he brought blues and swing to counter John Lewis's strict forms. He also made many records with others, such as Bags' Groove with Miles Davis and Bags & Trane with John Coltrane.
artiest/milt-jackson.listen: Notice the vibrato of the vibraphone: warm and singing.

artiest/milt-jackson-en-john-coltrane.text:
Milt Jackson & John Coltrane is the collaboration of two great names from modern jazz. Milt Jackson, nicknamed Bags, played vibraphone and was known as a member of the Modern Jazz Quartet. The saxophonist John Coltrane had already built up a considerable reputation by the late 1950s. He played in Miles Davis's quintet, worked briefly with Thelonious Monk in 1957 and took part in the recording of Kind of Blue in 1959. At Prestige he made his first albums as a leader, and in 1958 Blue Train was released on Blue Note.

In 1959 Coltrane signed with Atlantic Records. There he recorded, among others, Giant Steps and My Favorite Things. At almost all of those sessions he was the leader himself, with one exception: the album Bags & Trane, on which he can be heard together with Milt Jackson. The name of the record combines their nicknames. The album includes Be-Bop, a piece by Dizzy Gillespie from the early days of bebop. The music is fast and virtuosic: the warm, soft sound of the vibraphone is set against Coltrane's fierce, nimble saxophone. It is bebop as it had developed after the war: music to listen to, not to dance to. Shortly afterwards Coltrane struck out on a freer path of his own at Impulse!.
artiest/milt-jackson-en-john-coltrane.listen: Listen to Be-Bop and compare the solos of Milt Jackson on vibraphone and John Coltrane on saxophone. Notice the fast tempo and how both musicians race through the chords at express-train speed.

artiest/milton-babbitt.text:
Milton Babbitt (1916 to 2011) was an American composer, music theorist, mathematician and teacher. He was born in Philadelphia and grew up in Jackson, Mississippi. As a child he played violin, clarinet and saxophone, and he loved jazz and show music. He wrote arrangements of popular songs at an early age. His father was a mathematician, and that way of thinking continued to resonate in his music.

Babbitt studied in New York and with Roger Sessions, and from 1938 he was affiliated with Princeton University. He stayed there, with an interruption during the Second World War, teaching for decades; in 1973 a position at the Juilliard School was added. He became fascinated by the twelve-tone technique of Arnold Schoenberg and the Second Viennese School. He developed that technique into a system of his own and was a pioneer of integral serial music: not only the pitches, but also the rhythm and dynamics were built according to a fixed ordering. He also worked with the electronic music of the Columbia-Princeton Electronic Music Center, from which a record was released in 1961, and later recordings appeared of, among others, Philomel and Piano Works.

In 1958 his article appeared in the magazine High Fidelity, to which the editors gave the title Who Cares if You Listen?. It became a famous and controversial text about composers as researchers. Babbitt stood far from pop, but his influence was broad: among his students were the theatre composer Stephen Sondheim and the jazz guitarist Stanley Jordan.
artiest/milton-babbitt.listen: Listen to a section of Philomel and see whether you can remember a melody, or whether the music works more like a pattern of sounds that returns differently each time.

artiest/minmini.text:
Minmini is a singer from South India who became known above all as a playback singer for films. She was born on 12 August 1970 as P. J. Rosily in Keezhmedu, near Aluva in Kerala, and was the youngest of four sisters. At the age of five she began singing with Kalabhavan, a local orchestra. She made her film debut in 1989 with the Malayalam film Swagatham, for which she sang three songs.

In 1992 she moved into Tamil film. The composer Ilaiyaraaja brought her to Meera and gave her the name Minmini, which sounded more attractive to a Tamil audience. Her big breakthrough came that same year with Chinna Chinna Aasai from the film Roja, the debut work of the composer A. R. Rahman. The song became so popular that the place where it was recorded, the Paana Theertham Falls in the Tirunelveli district, attracted so many tourists that the government of Tamil Nadu closed the waterfalls to visitors for almost nine years to protect nature. The song also appeared in a Hindi version as Choti Si Asha.

Minmini sang mainly in Tamil, in songs by Ilaiyaraaja and Rahman, but also in Malayalam, Telugu and Kannada. In 1993 she lost her voice during a performance in London and could hardly speak for years. After treatment her voice returned, and in 2015 she made a comeback with Kanmaniye in the film Mili. With her husband, the keyboard player Joy Mathew, she founded a music school in Kochi.
artiest/minmini.listen: Listen to Chinna Chinna Aasai and notice how light and clear her voice sounds above the accompaniment of the film orchestra.

artiest/minor-threat.text:
Minor Threat was an American hardcore band from Washington, D.C. The singer Ian MacKaye and the drummer Jeff Nelson founded it in 1980, together with the guitarist Lyle Preslar and the bassist Brian Baker. In 1982 Steve Hansgen joined as bassist, after which Baker became second guitarist. MacKaye and Nelson had previously played in the Teen Idles and had used the money from that band to found the label Dischord Records. All of Minor Threat's records were released on it. Their first gig was in December 1980 in a basement, as support for Bad Brains.

The first EPs came out in 1981, Minor Threat and In My Eyes. Out of Step followed in 1983. The band lasted only three years. The music is short, fast and furious, with brief songs and screamed vocals. The song Straight Edge from the first EP is about MacKaye's choice not to use alcohol or other drugs, something that went against the rock culture of the time. Many later bands made it a way of life, and so the straight edge movement arose, although the band members themselves did not see it that way.

Minor Threat was regarded, together with Bad Brains and Black Flag, as the benchmark for the hardcore of the 1980s and 1990s. Just as important was the do-it-yourself attitude: the band released its own records and organised its own concerts. In this way it became a model for the independent punk scene.
artiest/minor-threat.listen: Listen to Straight Edge and notice how short the song is and how MacKaye delivers his lyrics almost screaming and without ceremony. Can you hear how the band does not stand still for a second?

artiest/miriam-makeba.text:
Zenzile Miriam Makeba (1932 to 2008) was a South African singer, songwriter and activist, known as Mama Africa. She was born in Johannesburg to a Swazi and a Xhosa parent. In the 1950s she began singing professionally with the Cuban Brothers, the Manhattan Brothers and the women's group the Skylarks, with a mixture of jazz, traditional African melodies and Western pop music. Her role in the anti-apartheid film Come Back, Africa brought her international attention in 1959.

In London she met Harry Belafonte, who became her mentor. She moved to New York and recorded her first solo record in 1960. When she wanted to go home that year for her mother's funeral, the South African government prevented it. Her best-known song became Pata Pata from 1967. With Belafonte she won a Grammy for the record An Evening With Belafonte/Makeba from 1965. She spoke against apartheid at the United Nations. After her marriage to Stokely Carmichael in 1968 the American government revoked her visa and she settled in Guinea. Only after the end of apartheid did she return to South Africa in 1990.

Makeba was one of the first African musicians with worldwide fame. She brought African music to a Western audience and contributed to the rise of world music and Afropop. Her songs against apartheid made her a symbol of resistance. She died in 2008 after a heart attack during a concert in Italy.
artiest/miriam-makeba.listen: Listen to Pata Pata and notice how her voice and the rhythm of the accompaniment keep complementing each other, and how cheerful this sounds for a singer who was not allowed to go home for years.

artiest/mirjam-timmer.text:
Mirjam Timmer is a Dutch singer-songwriter, born on 1 July 1982 in Leeuwarden. She comes from the Frisian village of Wergea, where she was already writing songs as a child. Together with fellow villager Johan van der Veen she took part in talent contests under the name Twarres. This led in 2000 to a number 1 hit in the Netherlands and Flanders with Wêr Bisto, a song in Frisian. The singles She Couldn't Laugh, Children and I Need To Know followed. The debut album Stream went platinum, and a second album, CD², was released later.

In 2003 Timmer wrote the music for the Frisian-language musical De lêste brief. Later that year she and Van der Veen decided to stop as a duo. A fall down some stairs, in which she broke her arm in 2004, meant for some time that she could not play guitar. She then worked with the producers John Themis and Gregor Hamilton in London on her solo debut.

From 2006 she performed solo under the name Mir, short for Mirjam. The first single Face to Face became a modest hit. Then came The Deep Blue Sea, on which she sings with Jim Kerr, the singer of Simple Minds. The solo album is called Files From London. Since 2015 she has been performing again as Twarres, with two new band members. Her career shows how a regional language in the Netherlands could become a national hit.
artiest/mirjam-timmer.listen: Listen to Wêr Bisto and notice how naturally a song in Frisian sounds as a pop song.

artiest/miroslav-vitous.text:
Miroslav Vitouš is a Czech jazz bassist, born on 6 December 1947 in Prague. He began on the violin at the age of six, switched to piano and at fourteen chose the double bass. He studied at the Prague Conservatoire and in 1966 won a competition in Vienna, which earned him a scholarship to Berklee in Boston. A year later he played in Chicago with Bob Brookmeyer and Clark Terry. There Miles Davis heard him and invited him to join his group in New York.

In the years that followed, Vitouš worked with Herbie Mann, Roy Haynes, Chick Corea, Jack DeJohnette, Wayne Shorter and Joe Zawinul. With Corea and Haynes he played on Now He Sings, Now He Sobs from 1968. In 1969 he recorded Infinite Search as a bandleader, with Herbie Hancock, Joe Henderson, John McLaughlin and DeJohnette. Purple followed in 1970.

In 1970 he formed the core of Weather Report with Shorter and Zawinul. The group gave every musician room to improvise continuously, instead of the usual division between soloist and accompaniment. Weather Report drew on influences from jazz, classical music, world music, rhythm and blues, funk and rock. Vitouš and Zawinul experimented with effects pedals, which until then had been used mainly by guitarists. Vitouš left the group in 1973 and afterwards remained a bandleader and collaborator of, among others, DeJohnette and Corea, with records such as Magical Shepherd, Emergence and Universal Syncopations.
artiest/miroslav-vitous.listen: Listen to Infinite Search and notice how the bass here does not merely keep time, but plays along almost like a second soloist.

artiest/mirza-abdollah.text:
Mirza Abdollah, in full Agha Mirza Abdollah Farahani (1843 to 1918), was an Iranian player of the tar and the setar, two stringed instruments from Persian classical music. He was born in Farahan. Together with his younger brother Mirza Hossein-Qoli he was taught by their father Ali-Akbar Farahani, himself a well-known musician. He is regarded as one of the most important musicians in the history of Iran.

His name is above all linked to the radif, the body of melodic models and pieces on which Persian classical music rests. His version for tar and setar became the best known and the most widely practised among contemporary Persian musicians. This was because he collected and ordered a large repertoire of traditional pieces, and because he liked to share his knowledge. He was a beloved teacher. His students included Abolhasan Saba, Esmaeil Ghahremani, Ali-Naqi Vaziri, Darvish Khan and Ahmad Ebadi.

His connection with the Baha'i Faith and with mystical orders was regarded as a source of his openness and generosity. Letters from 'Abdu'l-Bahá encouraged him to preserve and broaden classical music, and to shift its themes from sorrow and regret to hope and spiritual joy. In this way he became a key figure in the cultural revival that Iran experienced in the nineteenth century.
artiest/mirza-abdollah.listen: Listen to a recording of the tar in Persian classical music and notice how the melody moves freely back and forth, as if in conversation, without a fixed beat that you can tap along to.

artiest/misha-mengelberg.text: Misha (also Misja) Mengelberg was born in Kyiv and grew up in the Netherlands. He studied composition at the conservatoire in The Hague and was also involved in Fluxus. As a jazz pianist, Thelonious Monk was his great example. In 1964 he played with Eric Dolphy and Han Bennink the session that was released as Last Date. In 1967 he founded the Instant Composers Pool with Bennink and Willem Breuker. The ICP Orchestra played music by Monk, Herbie Nichols and Ellington alongside free improvisation and theatrical jokes. Mengelberg also campaigned for better conditions for improvisers in the Netherlands. He died in 2017.
artiest/misha-mengelberg.listen: Notice the ironic, halting piano phrases that recall Monk.

artiest/miss-kittin.text:
Miss Kittin is the stage name of Caroline Hervé, born on 16 July 1973 in Grenoble. She is a French producer, DJ, singer and songwriter. At home they played Genesis, Supertramp, Miles Davis, Maria Callas, Pink Floyd and The Beatles. She did ballet until she was twenty-two and studied art and graphic design. In 1993 she made her first mix, in 1994 came her first performance as a DJ, and in 1996 she moved to Geneva.

Her breakthrough came in 1998. In 1997 she had met DJ Hell, who wanted her to record for his label International DJ Gigolo. Together with The Hacker she made the singles 1982 and Frank Sinatra, which made her known in electronic music. Later she worked with Chicks on Speed, Felix da Housecat and Golden Boy. With Felix da Housecat she had international success with Rippin Kittin, and Silver Screen Shower Scene also became a well-known single.

Her first solo album I Com was released in 2004, followed by Batbox in 2008 and Calling From the Stars in 2013. Her music comes from the club: electronic rhythms and synthesizers, with a cool, almost spoken style of singing. In this way she belongs to the generation that gave the electronic dance music of around the turn of the millennium a face of its own.
artiest/miss-kittin.listen: Listen to Frank Sinatra and notice the interplay between the tight electronic beat and her vocals.

artiest/missy-elliott.text:
Missy Elliott is an American rapper, singer, songwriter and producer. She was born in 1971 in Portsmouth, Virginia, and grew up in a family where they sang in the church choir. Her childhood was hard: there was violence at home, and at fourteen she fled with her mother. In 1988 she started the girl group Fayze, later Sista, with friends. Through a neighbourhood friend she got to know Timothy Mosley, the producer who would become known as Timbaland. Sista ended up with the collective of DeVante Swing of Jodeci, but the group's album was never released.

From 1996 Elliott and Timbaland wrote and produced together for others, with the album One in a Million by Aaliyah as their greatest success. In 1997 came Elliott's own debut, Supa Dupa Fly. Da Real World (1999), Miss E... So Addictive (2001) with Get Ur Freak On, Under Construction (2002) with Work It, and The Cookbook (2005) with Lose Control followed. The beats of Timbaland and Elliott sounded different from all other hip-hop and R&B: stuttering, unexpected rhythms, strange sounds and a lot of space between the sounds. Elliott rapped and sang over them playfully and with great humour.

With her videos too she proved herself an innovator. She became the first female rapper in the Songwriters Hall of Fame and in 2023 in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. This makes her one of the few women in hip-hop who stood not only in front of the microphone, but also behind the controls.
artiest/missy-elliott.listen: Listen to Get Ur Freak On from 2001. Notice the tumbi, a Punjabi lute with a high, plucked motif, the tabla in the rhythm and the Japanese exclamation at the beginning.

artiest/mj-cole.text:
MJ Cole is really called Matthew James Firth Coleman and was born in 1973 in London. He received a classical training on oboe and piano and won scholarships to the Royal College of Music and the City of London School. After his studies he worked at the drum and bass label SOUR as a tape operator and sound engineer. Through the 2-step remixes by Ramsey and Fen for Kym Mazelle he caught the garage bug. Between 1997 and 1999 he was a regular engineer and producer at the UK garage label V.I.P. and a DJ on the pirate station London Underground FM.

In 1998 he wrote and produced Sincere with a sampler and an Atari. Via Pete Tong and AM:PM it became one of the first garage records in the British top forty. His album Sincere was released on Gilles Peterson's Talkin' Loud in 2000, earning him a Mercury Music Prize nomination and a Brit Award nomination, and in 2001 the MOBO for Best Producer, beating Dr. Dre. Cut to the Chase followed in 2003. Later he worked for, among others, Dizzee Rascal, Katy B and Mary J. Blige, and remixed Amy Winehouse and Mariah Carey.

UK garage is dance music from London with a swinging, broken rhythm, deep basses and soulful vocals. MJ Cole showed that a classical background and a club sound go well together, and contributed to the place of garage in British pop.
artiest/mj-cole.listen: Listen to Sincere and notice the rhythm that just does not run straight. Can you hear how the vocals make the song sound warm, while the beat underneath keeps skipping?

artiest/model-500.text:
Model 500 is the stage name of Juan Atkins, the producer and DJ from Detroit who is regarded as one of the founders of techno. Atkins was born in 1962 and as a child played guitar and bass in funk bands. In Belleville, near Detroit, he got to know Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson; together they are called the Belleville Three. At fifteen he bought a Korg MS-10 synthesizer.

In 1980 he started the duo Cybotron with Richard Davis, which released the track Clear in 1982 and the album Enter in 1983. In 1985 Atkins founded his own label, Metroplex, and under the name Model 500 released the records No UFO's and Night Drive. That music combined the funk of Parliament-Funkadelic with the electronic pop of Kraftwerk, and revealed a futuristic Detroit, coloured by dark science fiction. Later albums appeared under the name Model 500 such as Deep Space (1995), Mind and Body (1999) and Digital Solutions (2015).

AllMusic called Atkins the godfather of techno and his records perhaps the most influential work in the genre. What is characteristic is that his music, however mechanical, always keeps a strong melody. With Metroplex and Model 500 he laid a foundation for what later came to be called Detroit techno. Later he also worked with Moritz von Oswald in the duo Borderland.
artiest/model-500.listen: Listen in No UFO's to the tight drum machine and the bubbling synthesizer bass that drive the track forward. Notice the processed, robotic voice and how little changes: the tension lies in small shifts within the repetition.

artiest/model-500-juan-atkins.text:
Juan Atkins was born in 1962 in Detroit, Michigan. His father organised concerts and Atkins played guitar and bass guitar in funk bands with friends as a child. After his parents' divorce he moved to Belleville, Michigan. At high school he met Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, who together later came to be called the Belleville Three. At fifteen he bought his first synthesizer, a Korg MS-10.

In 1980 he founded the group Cybotron with Richard Davis, which released the album Enter in 1983. The track Clear from 1982 is regarded by AllMusic as the best starting point for techno. In 1985 the duo split up. That year Atkins founded the label Metroplex and began making solo records under the name Model 500, such as No UFO's. Later Deep Space (1995), Mind and Body (1999) and Digital Solutions (2015) followed under that name. Together with Moritz von Oswald he forms the duo Borderland.

His music fuses the cosmic side of Parliament and Funkadelic with the tight computer pop of Kraftwerk and with the visions of the future of the sociologist Alvin Toffler. He drew inspiration from dystopian science fiction and always showed a clear sense of melody in doing so. He grew up with the radio shows of The Electrifying Mojo. Mixmag calls him the original pioneer of Detroit techno, and AllMusic calls him the godfather of techno.
artiest/model-500-juan-atkins.listen: Listen to No UFO's and notice the cool synthesizer sounds and the tight rhythm of the drum machine. Can you hear that the melody has a character of its own, almost human, even though everything is electronic?

artiest/modern-jazz-quartet.text:
The Modern Jazz Quartet, MJQ for short, was founded in 1952. The group consisted of the pianist John Lewis, the vibraphonist Milt Jackson, the bassist Percy Heath and usually the drummer Kenny Clarke, later Connie Kay. They emerged from the rhythm section of Dizzy Gillespie's big band, where they played as a quartet during the intervals. Lewis became the musical director. In the first half of the 1950s they made records for Prestige, including the first versions of their two best-known compositions: Django by Lewis and Bags' Groove by Jackson. In 1956 the group moved to Atlantic and toured Europe for the first time.

Under Lewis's leadership they chose a path of their own: elegant, restrained music with ingenious Baroque counterpoint, but with a strong blues feeling. They were one of the first small jazz groups to perform in concert halls instead of nightclubs, and were known for their neat presentation. The quartet remained active until 1974, when Jackson left out of irritation over money and travel schedules, got together again in 1981 and continued until 1997. Albums such as Concorde (1955), Django (1956) and Fontessa (1956) belong to the early years.

The MJQ combined classical music, Cool Jazz, blues and bebop. Through their controlled sound and their sense of form they showed that jazz could also sound like chamber music, without losing its swing.
artiest/modern-jazz-quartet.listen: Listen to Django and notice how vibraphone and piano pass melodies to each other, while bass and drums calmly keep the tempo. Can you hear the classical form, and the blues as well?

artiest/modern-talking.text:
Modern Talking was a German pop duo of the arranger, songwriter and producer Dieter Bohlen and the singer Thomas Anders. They began in the spring of 1983 in West Berlin. They only became really well known in early 1985 with You're My Heart, You're My Soul, which reached the top ten in at least fifteen countries and was number one in Germany for six weeks. That year You Can Win If You Want from the debut album The 1st Album followed, and then Cheri, Cheri Lady from Let's Talk About Love.

In a short time more hits came: Brother Louie and Atlantis Is Calling (S.O.S. for Love) from Ready for Romance, Geronimo's Cadillac from In the Middle of Nowhere and Jet Airliner from Romantic Warriors. The music is simple and radio-oriented: a clear, light pop sound with plenty of synthesizers, with melodies you can sing along to after hearing them once. Bohlen wrote and produced, Anders sang.

After a poorly received sixth album, In the Garden of Venus, Bohlen announced the end of the project in 1987. The relationship between the two had long been strained. In 1998 they made a successful comeback with a new version of You're My Heart, You're My Soul, and released more albums until 2003, with the participation of the rapper Eric Singleton. After that they split up for good. They are regarded as the most successful German pop duo, and show how German pop music in the 1980s conquered much of Europe.
artiest/modern-talking.listen: Listen to You're My Heart, You're My Soul and notice how simply the melody and chorus are built, and how much room the synthesizers get in the sound.

artiest/modest-moessorgski.text: Modest Mussorgsky was an officer and later a civil servant in St Petersburg and belonged to the Group of Five, composers who wanted a Russian music of their own. He had little formal training and let himself be guided by the sound of the Russian language and folk music instead of Western rules. His Pictures at an Exhibition from 1874 describes a walk past the work of his late friend Viktor Hartmann. His opera Boris Godunov became a model for Debussy.
artiest/modest-moessorgski.listen: Listen to the Promenade and hear how the time signature keeps changing, as if you were walking through a museum gallery with irregular steps.

artiest/mohammad-reza-lotfi.text:
Mohammad-Reza Lotfi (1947 to 2014) was an Iranian musician who was known for his mastery of the tar and the setar, two stringed instruments from Persian classical music. He was born in Gorgan, in a cultured family in which both parents were teachers. His older brother encouraged him to learn the tar, and in 1964 he won first prize at the Iranian festival for young musicians. A year later he began at the Persian national conservatoire in Tehran, where Habibollah Salehi and Ali Akbar Shahnazi were his teachers. Abdollah Davami taught him the radif, the traditional repertoire, and Said Hormozi taught him the setar.

Lotfi played in the orchestra of the Department of Fine Arts, studied at the University of Tehran and after graduating in 1973 taught there himself. He co-founded the Shayda Ensemble and led, among other things, the centre that preserved and disseminated traditional Persian music. From 1978 to 1980 he was head of the university's music school. He then lived for two years in Italy and from 1986 in the United States, and performed in Asia, Europe and North America.

He made many recordings, solo and with great Iranian musicians such as Mohammad Reza Shajarian, Shahram Nazeri, Hossein Alizadeh and Parviz Meshkatian. He made a record with the singer Hengameh Akhavan. Lotfi is regarded as one of the greatest contemporary masters of the tar and setar and as one of the figures who renewed Persian classical music in recent decades.
artiest/mohammad-reza-lotfi.listen: Listen to a recording of Lotfi on the tar or setar, for example from Mystery of Love, and notice how a single string is given room to sing, without the piece needing a fixed beat.

artiest/mohammad-reza-lotfi-en-mohammad-.text:
Mohammad-Reza Shajarian was born in 1940 in Mashhad, Iran. His father was a Quran reciter and taught him singing technique at the age of five, at first through Quran recitation. At twelve, without his father knowing, he began studying Persian classical music, the radif. His teachers included Ahmad Ebadi, Esmaeil Mehrtash, Abdollah Davami and Nour-Ali Boroumand. In 1959 he began singing at Radio Khorasan, and in the 1960s he grew into a well-known name.

He was regarded as a master of the difficult dastgah style and worked with many musicians, among them Parviz Meshkatian, Mohammad Reza Lotfi, Hossein Alizadeh, Kayhan Kalhor and his son Homayoun Shajarian. He taught at the University of Tehran, worked for national radio and television and carried out research into Persian music. After the revolution of 1979 he was one of the few singers who were allowed to continue singing in public. After he supported the Green Movement and criticised the government, he was banned from concerts and releases. He received the Picasso Award in 1999 and the UNESCO Mozart Medal in 2006. He died in 2020.

In the Persian classical tradition the singer determines much of what is played. The music is built on melodic models, the dastgahs, within which the musicians improvise. A daramad is the opening section of such a dastgah, in which the tone is set.
artiest/mohammad-reza-lotfi-en-mohammad-.listen: Listen to Daramad (Abu-Ata) and notice the dialogue between the voice and the stringed instrument. Can you hear how the singer sings long, ornate lines, and how the instrument answers and completes them?

artiest/mohammad-reza-shajarian.text: Mohammad-Reza Shajarian was born in Mashhad and became the most important singer of Persian classical music. He mastered the old ornaments of the avaz, the free singing of Persian poetry, down to the smallest tremor. His sung prayer Rabbana was heard every year during Ramadan on Iranian radio from 1979. After the elections of 2009 he sided with the protesters, after which the state broadcaster banned his music.
artiest/mohammad-reza-shajarian.listen: Listen in the concert with the tar player Mohammad Reza Lotfi to how the voice and the tar alternate: the tar repeats and answers what Shajarian has just sung.

artiest/mohammed-abdel-wahab.text: Mohammed Abdel Wahab was a singer, oud player and composer in Cairo and made his first recordings as a child. From 1933 he acted in musical films, beginning with The White Rose, and he brought in rhythms from outside Arabic music, such as a waltz in El Gandol (1941). For Oum Kalthoum he wrote ten songs, including Anta Oumri (1964). In this way he linked the old tarab with film, radio and the modern orchestra.
artiest/mohammed-abdel-wahab.listen: Listen to Etab and hear how his soft, supple voice sings the ornamented melody, while the orchestra answers every phrase.

artiest/mohammed-rafi.text:
Mohammed Rafi was born in 1924 into a Punjabi family in the village of Kotla Sultan Singh near Amritsar. He began singing by imitating the songs of a wandering fakir. His father moved to Lahore in 1935, where he had a barber's shop. Rafi learned classical music from Ustad Abdul Wahid Khan and others. He gave his first performance at thirteen, and in 1941 he made his debut as a playback singer in a Punjabi film. In 1944 he moved to Bombay, where he rented a small room in Bhendi Bazar. His first recorded song in a Hindi film was a duet for Gaon Ki Gori.

Rafi became one of the most sought-after singers in Hindi film. He often worked with the composer Naushad Ali, and later also with O. P. Nayyar, Shankar Jaikishan, S.D. Burman and Roshan. He recorded songs for more than a thousand Hindi films and in many languages, mainly Urdu and Punjabi. He received six Filmfare Awards and a National Film Award, and in 1967 the Padma Shri.

His voice was versatile. He sang fast and cheerful numbers, sad and romantic songs, qawwali, ghazals, bhajans and classical pieces. Moreover, he adapted his voice to the actor who lip-synced the song on screen. That made him one of the most important voices of Indian film music and of the golden age of Hindi film. He died in 1980.
artiest/mohammed-rafi.listen: Listen to Yeh Duniya Agar Mil Bhi Jaye and notice how he sings the words. Can you hear the emotion in his voice, even when he sings softly?

artiest/moki-cherry.text:
Moki Cherry (1943 to 2009) was a Swedish artist and designer. She was born Monika Marianne Karlsson in Koler in northern Sweden, the daughter of the stationmaster and the postal clerk. In 1962 she went to Stockholm to study fashion and textiles at Beckman's School of Design, where she specialised in illustration, patterns and clothing. In 1964 she had a daughter, Neneh, who later became a singer herself.

In 1963 she met the American jazz trumpeter Don Cherry, when he was on tour with Sonny Rollins in Stockholm. In the years that followed they became a couple. After graduating in 1966 she travelled to New York and their lifelong collaboration began. She worked with textiles, painting, woodwork, collage, ceramics, fashion and set design. Her colourful tapestries formed the setting for Don's performances and adorned his record sleeves, such as those of Brown Rice, Relativity Suite and Organic Music Society. The clothes he wore on stage also came from her.

The couple performed under the name Organic Music, with her artworks on display, and gave workshops for children. Her work drew on influences from Indian art and music, Tibetan Buddhism, folk art, abstraction, comics and pop art. From 1977 she lived alternately in Tågarp in Sweden and in Long Island City in New York. She shows how closely visual art and jazz were intertwined in the 1960s and 1970s.
artiest/moki-cherry.listen: While listening to a record by Don Cherry, such as Brown Rice, also look at the sleeve Moki designed, and notice whether the colours and patterns fit the open, playful sound of the music.
